pinterest.title: Rabbit White Korma with Cashew Cream — Halal French-Pakistani Fusion
pinterest.description: Rabbit white korma reimagined: French lapin slow-braised until it surrenders, then finished in a silky cashew cream sauce laced with white pepper and whole spices. No shortcuts, no approximations. This halal fusion recipe marries classical French braising with the restraint of a pale korma — delicate, layered, and quietly extraordinary. Full method on mubashirr.com

instagram.caption:
There is a version of korma that never raises its voice. No turmeric staining the pot, no chilli heat pushing to the front. Just white pepper, cashew cream, and time.

This is rabbit white korma — lapin braised low and slow in the French tradition, then pulled into a sauce that belongs to both worlds without being fully claimed by either. The cashew does what heavy cream sometimes cannot: it holds the spice without drowning it, thickens without weighing, and gives the finished dish a colour somewhere between ivory and pale gold.

Rabbit is forgiving when you treat it correctly. It wants low heat, patience, and enough liquid to keep it honest. Rush it and the meat tightens. Give it time and it falls from the bone in long, clean pieces that take the sauce like they were made for it.

The full method — quantities, timing, technique — is linked in my bio. Worth the read before you start.

email.subject: The korma that whispers
email.preheader: Rabbit braised low and slow, finished in cashew cream and white pepper.
email.body_html:
Most korma arrives with colour — turmeric yellow, chilli red, the visible evidence of spice. This one does not.

Rabbit white korma is built on restraint. The heat comes from white pepper rather than red, the body from cashew cream rather than yoghurt thinned with water, and the depth from a braise that runs low and slow until the lapin gives up all resistance and falls cleanly from the bone.

The French technique is not decoration here. Braising rabbit correctly — covering it partially, maintaining a gentle simmer, turning it at intervals — is what separates a dish with good ingredients from a dish worth returning to. Too much heat and the meat seizes. Too little time and it stays politely firm when it should be yielding.

The korma element brings the whole spices, the cashew paste, the precise ratio of cream to stock that keeps the sauce from tipping into either richness or water. It is fusion in the older sense of the word: two traditions applied with equal seriousness, not one raiding the other for aesthetics.

I have written the full method with quantities, timing notes, and a few things worth knowing before you start. If you cook it once, you will understand why rabbit belongs in this sauce.

Read the full recipe and method here.

linkedin.body:
Fusion cooking fails most often at the seam — the place where two traditions are supposed to meet but instead simply collide. One technique overwhelms the other, or both are diluted until neither is recognisable.

Rabbit white korma was an exercise in avoiding exactly that.

The French contribution is structural: lapin braised low and slow, partially submerged, turned carefully, coaxed rather than cooked. French technique applied to rabbit is not a novelty — it is simply the correct way to treat meat that tightens under high heat and rewards patience with texture that no other method produces.

The korma logic runs alongside it without compromise. White pepper instead of red. Cashew cream built from scratch, not approximated with store-bought paste. Whole spices added at the right stage so they perfume the braising liquid without monopolising it.

What results is a dish that is pale, quiet, and more complex than either parent recipe alone. The cashew cream carries the spice without obscuring it. The rabbit absorbs the sauce in a way that chicken, for all its convenience, simply does not.

I wrote the full recipe and technique breakdown on the blog — including the points in the process where most cooks cut corners and what it costs them.

Link in the comments for anyone who wants to read it properly.

tweets: I made a korma that has no colour. No turmeric, no red. Just white pepper, cashew cream, and a French braise running low and slow until the rabbit stops resisting. Thread.

Rabbit tightens fast under the wrong heat. The French know this. You braise it partially submerged, gentle simmer, turned at intervals. The meat falls long and clean from the bone. That texture is the foundation — get it wrong and the sauce cannot save you.

The korma side of this is built on restraint too. Cashew paste made properly, not approximated. White pepper doing the work that chilli usually does loudly. Whole spices added early enough to perfume the liquid, late enough not to dominate it.

What you get is pale, quiet, and layered in a way that takes a few bites to fully understand. Fusion that works not because it is clever but because both techniques were applied seriously. Neither tradition is decorative here.
Full recipe and method — quantities, timing, the steps worth slowing down for — on the blog: https://mubashirr.com/rabbit-white-korma-cashew-cream/

Lapin braised low and slow, finished with white pepper and whole spices — it sits somewhere between two traditions without belonging entirely to either one, which is exactly where it should be.
